cls: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist (long-acting; once-weekly injectable antidiabetic)
pharm: GLP-1 receptor agonist that enhances glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon, and slows gastric emptying, lowering fasting and postprandial glucose.

summary: Dulaglutide is a once-weekly subcutaneous GLP-1 receptor agonist used as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in type 2 diabetes (adults and children 10 years and older), and to reduce cardiovascular events in adults with established cardiovascular disease or risk factors. It works in a glucose-dependent manner, so it rarely causes hypoglycemia alone but increases hypoglycemia risk with sulfonylureas or insulin. It carries a BOXED WARNING for thyroid C-cell tumors (medullary thyroid carcinoma seen in rodents) and is contraindicated in personal/family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2. The most common adverse effects are gastrointestinal (nausea, diarrhea, vomiting), and pancreatitis is a recognized risk.
indications: Adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults and pediatric patients 10 years and older with type 2 diabetes mellitus
Reduction of major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus who have established cardiovascular disease or multiple cardiovascular risk factors

moa: Dulaglutide is a recombinant fusion protein consisting of two GLP-1 analog molecules linked to a modified human IgG4 Fc fragment, which prolongs its half-life and allows once-weekly dosing. As a GLP-1 receptor agonist, it potentiates glucose-dependent insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells, suppresses inappropriately elevated glucagon secretion, and slows gastric emptying. Because insulin release is glucose-dependent, it lowers glucose with low intrinsic risk of hypoglycemia. The slowing of gastric emptying and central effects also reduce appetite and promote modest weight loss, and the class confers cardiovascular benefit.

Known serious hypersensitivity to dulaglutide or any component
relative: History of pancreatitis (not studied; use caution)
Severe gastrointestinal disease, including severe gastroparesis
monitor: Symptoms of thyroid tumors (neck mass, dysphagia, dyspnea, hoarseness)
Signs of pancreatitis (persistent severe abdominal pain)
Renal function with severe GI adverse reactions/dehydration

preg: There are limited human data. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus; animal studies showed developmental abnormalities at exposures above the human dose. Discontinuation may be considered as pregnancy approaches given the long half-life.
lact: There are no data on the presence of dulaglutide in human milk or its effects on the breastfed infant or milk production; the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be considered along with the mother's clinical need and any potential adverse effects.
renal: No dose adjustment is required for renal impairment, but monitor renal function in patients who experience severe gastrointestinal adverse reactions (which can cause dehydration and acute kidney injury).
hepatic: There is limited clinical experience in hepatic impairment; use with caution.

major: Insulin and insulin secretagogues (sulfonylureas) - increased hypoglycemia risk; consider lowering their dose
moderate: Oral medications - delayed gastric emptying can alter the rate of absorption; monitor narrow-therapeutic-index oral drugs (e.g., warfarin) and those dependent on threshold concentrations
Oral medications requiring rapid GI absorption may have reduced effect
minor: At the 1.5 mg dose, absorption of tested oral drugs was not affected to a clinically relevant degree
interactions.food: May be given with or without food at any time of day.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol; it can impair glycemic control and may contribute to pancreatitis risk.
interactions.diagnostics: May elevate serum lipase and amylase; interpret in clinical context for pancreatitis.

serious: Acute kidney injury from severe GI losses/dehydration
rare: Medullary thyroid carcinoma (rodent finding; human risk unknown)
emergency: Symptoms suggestive of a thyroid tumor

counsel: Inject under the skin once a week on the same day; you can change the day as long as doses are at least 3 days apart
Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea are common at first and usually improve - eat smaller meals and stay hydrated
Seek urgent care for severe, persistent stomach pain that may spread to your back (possible pancreas inflammation)
Tell your doctor about any lump in your neck, trouble swallowing, or persistent hoarseness
If you also use insulin or a sulfonylurea, watch for low blood sugar and carry fast-acting sugar
Rotate injection sites and never share your pen
pk: Glucose-lowering observed after the first dose; full effect builds over weeks
Median Tmax ~24-72 hours (about 48 hours) at steady state
Once-weekly dosing; steady state in 2-4 weeks
Refrigerate at 2-8 C; may keep at room temperature up to 30 C for up to 14 days; do not freeze; protect from light
pearls: BOXED WARNING: thyroid C-cell tumors - contraindicated with personal/family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2
Once-weekly dosing thanks to Fc fusion and ~5-day half-life; can switch the dosing day if doses are >=3 days apart
Glucose-dependent action means low hypoglycemia risk alone - reduce insulin/sulfonylurea to avoid lows
GI effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea) are the most common reason for discontinuation; titrate and hydrate
Recognized risks of pancreatitis and gallbladder disease - educate on warning symptoms
Provides cardiovascular benefit in patients with established CVD or multiple risk factors
missed: If you miss a weekly dose, take it as soon as possible if at least 3 days (72 hours) remain until the next scheduled dose. If fewer than 3 days remain, skip the missed dose and take the next dose on the regular day. Do not take two doses within 3 days of each other.
overdose: Overdoses in clinical trials produced primarily mild to moderate gastrointestinal events and non-severe hypoglycemia. There is no specific antidote; treatment is supportive with appropriate clinical monitoring, including frequent blood glucose measurement, given the long half-life.
